text: Every time a coding agent starts a task, it explores the repository from scratch. Every search and every file it opens is paid for in tokens.
And most of that exploration repeats what a teammate's agent already found last week.
Bearings remembers where past work landed, as a graph in HydraDB.
Each finished task is written as structure: the words and symbols in it, the files it changed, and the test that verified it.
When a new task arrives, one weighted path query walks from its words to files, and returns a small context pack. Where to start, how to test, and the path that justifies each file.
It also looks up where the names in the task are defined in today's code, so the pack points to the exact lines to read.
Links that led to the right file get cheaper. Links that led nowhere get dearer. And Bearings makes no model calls, so the layer itself is free to run.

We replayed every Django issue from SWE-bench in date order. Bearings ranked the real fix first about half the time, ahead of keyword search, and had it in the top five more than three times out of four.
Starting from an empty graph, it learns as issues arrive, and pulls well ahead of keyword search.
Here is one new issue. With the pack, the agent went to the right lines and was done in ten tool calls instead of nineteen.
Across forty new issues, though, it saved nothing. Those issues already point at the code, so the agent finds the file in its first step either way.
Claude Code told the same story on our two demo tasks. Where Bearings wins is ranking: which file to open first, and learning from an empty start.
And we report what did not help. The second hop, through files that change together, barely moves the results.
It is built for teams that share a repository. What one person's agent learns, every agent on the team starts from.
Bearings. Your agents start where your team left off.
